Poaceae Zea Mays True Gold Corn Start outdoors after your last expected frost date. Sow seeds 1 inch below the surface. Prefers average soils, acidic to neutral pH, and full sun.

Fabaceae Phaseolus Vulgaris Purple Peacock Pole Bean Start outdoors 2 weeks after planting the corn. Sow seeds 1 inch below the surface within several inches of the corn. Prefers average soils, acidic to neutral pH, and full sun to part shade. These climbing beans will use the corn stalks for support, and in turn anchor the corn in the ground during windy conditions. The roots of the beans will provide nitrogen needed by surrounding plants.

Cucurbitaceae Cucurbita Pepo var. Turbinata Table Queen Acorn Squash Start seeds indoors 3 weeks prior to your last expected frost date. Sow seeds 1 inch below the surface and keep warm and moist. Prefers average soils, no specific pH, and full sun to part shade. The squash will form a layer of living mulch around the roots of the corn, protecting it from drying out and preventing weeds that will compete for nutrients.

Asteraceae Cichorium Endivia Full Heart Batavian Endive Start seeds indoors 6 week prior to your last expected frost date. Sow seeds just under the surface and keep moist. Very prone to damping off, so do not over water and allow plenty of air circulation. Once established they are very hardy. Prefers average soils, no specific pH, and part shade. The endive will thrive in the shade created by the corn and provide crisp and hardier greens up until a hard freeze.

Umbelliferae Foeniculum Vulgare Florence Fennel Start seeds indoors 10 weeks prior to your last expected frost date. Sow seeds 1/4 inch below the surface. Prefers average soils, no specific pH, and full sun. While fennel does not directly help plants near it, quite the opposite, it does attract large numbers of predatory wasps when in bloom. These will both polinate the beans and squash, and kill non beneficial insects. Once the fennel is harvested, mulch the root crown heavily in fall and the plant should resurface in the spring.

Asteraceae Helianthus Annuus Evening Sunflower Start outdoors after your last expected frost date. Sow seeds 1/2 inch below the surface. Prefers average soils, no specific pH, and full sun to part shade. Sunflowers attract pollinators and lacewings, as well as providing additional support to climbing beans.

Coreopsideae Cosmos Bipinnatus Sensation Cosmo Start outdoors after your last expected frost date. Sow seeds 1/4 inch below the surface. prefers average soils, no specific pH, and full sun to part shade. Cosmos attract a large variety of insects and polinators who can lay eggs and create nests in its foliage. This helps reduce corn worms as these insects will feed off corn worm eggs lain on corn silk.

Tomato Guild

https://imgoat.com/uploads/3ec517d68b/80481.pngPNG

Solanaceae Lycopersicon Lycopersicum True Black Brandywine Tomato Start indoors 8-6 weeks prior to your last expected frost date. Sow seeds just under the surface. Transplant after your last frost once the soil has warmed up a bit. Prefers average soils, acidic to neutral pH, and full sun.

Tropaeolaceae Tropaeolum Majus Mixed Nasturtiums Sow seeds outdoors after your last expected frost date, 1/4 inch below the surface. Prefers average soils, no specific pH, and full sun to part shade. The leaves and flowers are edible, and the seeds can be harvested and pickled in the same way as capers. The nasturtium will act as a living mulch to cover and protect the soil and increas humidity around the base of the tomato.

Alliaceae Allium Ampeloprasum Musselburgh Leek Start indoors 12 weeks prior to your last expected frost date. Sow seeds 1/4 below the surface. Transplant outside after your last frost. Dig a trench approximately half the depth of the seedlings. Place the seedlings in the trench about 4 inches apart and gently backfill. As the leeks grow, mound up soil along the trench. Prefers average to rich soil, no specific pH, and full sun. If some leeks are left in the ground to go to seed and grow perennially, they act as a fungicide on the soil. This is beneficial to tomato plants in the following year.

Lamiaceae Ocimum Basilicum Corsican Basil Start indoors 6 weeks prior to your last expected frost date. Sow seeds just under the surface. Transplant after your last frost once the soil has warmed up a bit. Prefers average soils, no specific pH, and full sun to part shade. The potent scent of basil repels many small insects such as mites and aphids. Once in bloom, the flowers attract polinating bees and predatory wasps.

Umbelliferae Daucus Carota Queen Anne's Lace Sow seeds outdoors 2 weeks prior to your last expected frost date. Mix into the surface and keep moist. Prefers loamy soils, no specific pH, and full sun to part shade. In heavier soils, the root of queen anne's lace will slowly aid in breaking apart the soil. The plant is a biennial and will not produce flowers in the first year. Once it does produce flowers, it attracts large quantities of predatory wasps that attack cabbage and tomato worms. The best practice is to sow seeds every year, so that by the second year you have a continual flower presence attracting wasps.

Asteraceae Tagetes Erecta Marigold Start seeds indoors 4 weeks priorr to your last expected frost date. Mix into the surface and keep moist. Prefers average soils, no specific pH, and full sun to part shade. Marigolds are reported to deter harmful nematodes from attacking the roots of tomato plants, but generally are more effective at attracting beneficial insects. Deer seem detered by them, so they work well as a low border to reduce browsing pressure on other plants.

Grossulariaceae Ribes Uva-crispa var. Reclinatum Invicta Gooseberry Keep cuttings refrigerated and wrapped in a moist(not wet) paper towel until ready to plant. These can be planted immediately upon receipt as long as the ground is thawed enough to work, or started indoors to get an earlier start on rooting. When ready to plant in the ground, dig a small hole and work the soil until well loosened. Plant the cutting with at least three inches below the soil, and mulch around the exposed portion of the cutting. If possible, place a cloche or clear plastic bottle over the cutting to keep humidity in. The cutting will take several years to produce fruit. Tomatoes will help protect the gooseberry from insect damage, and the gooseberry will eventually be large enough to discourage deer from browsing the more tender plants around it.
